strengths: Well-motivated identification of geometric perception as an under-evaluated MLLM capability with clear practical relevance
Systematic and large-scale benchmark: 80K images, 285K questions with rigorous data synthesis pipeline, balanced aspect coverage, and human validation (99.3% accuracy)
Comprehensive empirical evaluation of 20 models with thorough ablations on visual encoders, complexity factors, and noise impact
Clear identification of specific limitations: size and location tasks particularly challenging; limited scaling benefits; visual encoder trade-offs between resolution and spatial accuracy
Strong reproducibility foundation: detailed algorithm specification, published training procedures, commitment to release code and data
weaknesses: Scope limitation: 'Geometric perception' narrowly defined for synthetic basic shapes; unclear generalization to real-world geometric understanding in natural images or complex diagrams

Modest practical significance: LLaVA-GeP shows only 2.2% average improvement on downstream tasks; training data mixing confounds attribution; missing control experiment with non-geometric synthetic data

Incomplete failure analysis: No investigation why state-of-the-art models score below random (17.5%) on size tasks; limited error breakdown by shape type; encoder bottleneck explanations remain speculative

Evaluation constraints: Zero-shot only (no few-shot/fine-tuning); multiple-choice format vulnerable to distractor exploitation; answer parsing validated on only 100 samples; no statistical significance testing

Data synthesis underspecification: Algorithm 1 vague on relationship enforcement; no analysis of relationship frequency balance; template-based QA generation may enable pattern exploitation rather than true understanding

Confounded improvement attribution: Data mixing of GePBench with original LLaVA training makes isolated contribution unclear; Figure 6 shows inconsistent gains across tasks; some improvements within noise margins

Limited comparative analysis: Missing comparison of MLLM performance on GePBench versus existing geometry datasets (GeoQA, Geometry3K); unexpected noise results (Figure 10) inadequately explained; narrow focus on transformer-based vision models

strengths: Clearly motivated research gap: Identifies that existing MLLM benchmarks overlook fundamental geometric perception despite its foundational importance
Comprehensive empirical evaluation: Systematic assessment of 20 diverse MLLMs (closed and open-source) with consistent methodology and detailed model documentation
Systematic benchmark construction: Well-designed data synthesis pipeline (Algorithm 1) with structured description generation, figure rendering, and QA generation
Rigorous experimental design: Includes human evaluation, ablation studies on visual encoders, model scaling analysis, and downstream task evaluation from multiple angles

Striking empirical findings: Clear demonstration that state-of-the-art models (GPT-4o: 17.5% on size) catastrophically fail below random guessing, revealing substantial human-model gap (>40%) on simple tasks
Detailed reproducibility documentation: Extensive appendices providing implementation details, model sources, evaluation protocols, and training procedures
weaknesses: Limited downstream improvements undermine core claims: Only 2.2% average improvement on math/chart benchmarks is insufficient to support claims that geometric perception is 'foundational' or 'pivotal' to MLLM capabilities

Insufficient novelty in benchmark design: Template-based QA generation over synthetic figures is straightforward; the distinction from prior geometry benchmarks (GeoQA, Geometry3K, UniGeo) regarding 'perception vs. reasoning' is unconvincing and not empirically validated

Weak practical significance and artificial task design: Figures are highly synthetic Matplotlib-rendered shapes; connection to claimed applications (medical imaging, fossil classification) is assumed rather than demonstrated; no evidence these specific geometric tasks bottleneck real-world applications

Contradictory noise analysis undermines methodology: Figure 10 shows noise actually improves performance for several models (Gemini, mPLUG-Owl, InternVL), contradicting claims that noise simulates real-world degradation and questioning appropriateness of the benchmark design

Limited human evaluation rigor: Only 5 undergraduate volunteers; 200 questions per aspect per split; no inter-rater agreement statistics; suspiciously homogeneous 99.3% accuracy without individual score reporting

Insufficient mechanistic analysis of model failures: Paper shows models fail but provides limited evidence for claimed causes (visual encoder invariance); lacks detailed failure mode analysis or actionable insights for improvement

Incomplete downstream validation: No ablation comparing geometric perception data vs. random additional training data; improvements concentrated in only 3 of 12 benchmark categories; individual improvements range 0-3%, raising questions about practical significance
Missing critical comparisons: No head-to-head evaluation on shared benchmarks with related geometry datasets (GeoQA, Geometry3K); no evidence GePBench is uniquely valuable

Weak analysis of visual encoders (Table 2): Findings are contradictory and mechanistically unclear; why does higher resolution hurt location tasks? Why do mixed encoders underperform? Explanations are speculative
No statistical rigor: Absence of confidence intervals, significance tests, inter-rater agreement statistics, or variance analysis across multiple runs

Limited training methodology novelty: LLaVA-GeP uses standard training pipeline with synthetic data; no architectural innovations, novel loss functions, or principled approaches to improving geometric perception

Data synthesis limitations underexplored: Overlap threshold mechanism is simplistic; only 9 geometric relationships and 10 shape types; no ablation on these design choices; unclear if model failures reflect geometric perception deficiency or Matplotlib rendering artifacts

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing a genuine gap in MLLM evaluation: geometric perception remains underexplored despite being foundational to visual understanding
Systematic and reproducible benchmark construction: clear data synthesis pipeline (Algorithm 1) with structured textual descriptions ensuring consistency
Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 20 models (closed and open-source), proper zero-shot protocol, 99.9% answer parsing accuracy, multiple ablation studies

Compelling findings: SOTA models score below random guessing on size (GPT-4o: 17.5%), revealing critical limitations; insightful observation that scaling provides diminishing returns compared to general benchmarks
Rigorous validation: human evaluation (99.3% accuracy) confirms task quality; large-scale dataset (80K images, 285K questions) with balanced splits and multiple aspects
Demonstrated downstream value: training on GePBench improves performance on real-world benchmarks, supporting the foundational importance claim
Clear presentation and excellent reproducibility documentation: well-written paper with informative figures, comprehensive appendices with implementation details
weaknesses: Limited human evaluation: only 5 undergraduate volunteers, no inter-rater agreement reported, limited demographic diversity, small sample size may not fully capture human performance variation
Modest downstream improvements without significance testing: 2.2% average gain on math/chart benchmarks; unclear whether improvements stem from geometric perception or simply more training data
Fully synthetic benchmark may not reflect real-world geometric perception: all images rendered with Matplotlib; limited diversity in visual characteristics compared to natural geometric tasks
Incomplete analysis of failure modes: speculative explanations for why some models improve with noise (Section E.2), limited investigation of specific error categories or shape confusion patterns

Underspecified design details: distractor generation strategy varies across aspects but lacks rigor; simple overlap checking in Algorithm 1 doesn't ensure diverse configurations; easy/hard distinction is binary rather than graduated

Limited technical novelty: straightforward template-based data synthesis; LLaVA-GeP simply fine-tunes existing architecture; identifies problems (invariance vs. spatial sensitivity in encoders) but proposes no architectural solutions

Methodological concerns: no analysis of question aspect interdependencies, no distractor difficulty analysis, impact of question length not studied, potential test set leakage from synthetic data not discussed
